# Board pack: ten security metrics for the board

<!-- Generated by scripts/build_catalogue.py from data/metrics.yaml. Do not edit by hand. -->

A board does not need forty metrics. It needs ten that answer three questions: *are we protected against the attacks that matter*, *would we notice and recover*, and *are we meeting our obligations*. Each metric below is shown with a plain-language narrative, the target, and the question a director can ask to test the number.

Present each metric the same way every quarter: current value, previous quarter, target, 12-month trend (a sparkline is enough), and one sentence of commentary. Do not change definitions between quarters without saying so.

## The ten, on one page

| # | Metric | Answers the question | Target (example) | Frequency |
|---|--------|----------------------|------------------|-----------|
| 1 | **MFA coverage (all users)** (IDN-01) | Can accounts be taken over with just a password? | >= 99 % | Monthly |
| 2 | **Critical vulnerabilities remediated within SLA** (VUL-01) | Do we fix the dangerous weaknesses in time? | >= 90 % within 14 days | Monthly |
| 3 | **EDR coverage** (END-01) | Are our devices watched? | >= 98 % | Monthly |
| 4 | **Mean time to contain** (DR-02) | How fast do we shut an attacker out? | <= 4 hours for High and Critical incidents | Quarterly |
| 5 | **Security incidents by severity** (DR-06) | What actually happened this period? | 0 Critical; trend of High and Medium flat or down | Monthly |
| 6 | **Phishing simulation click rate** (AWR-01) | Would our people fall for a fake email? | <= 5 % (with difficulty level held constant) | Monthly |
| 7 | **Tier 1 vendors assessed within cadence** (TPR-01) | Are our critical suppliers checked? | 100 % | Quarterly |
| 8 | **Control coverage against framework** (GOV-03) | How much of our security framework is really in place? | >= 85 % implemented, 100 % of Critical-priority controls | Quarterly |
| 9 | **Backup restore test success** (CLD-04) | Could we recover from a destructive attack? | 100 % per year, >= 25 % per quarter on rotation | Quarterly |
| 10 | **AI systems with a completed impact assessment** (AI-02) | Was our AI checked for harm before go-live? | 100 % before go-live | Quarterly |

## How to read the pack

- **Leading** indicators (coverage, hygiene) predict future incidents; **lagging** ones (incidents, containment time) record what happened. A healthy pack has both, and the leading ones should move first.
- Arrows show direction against target, not against last quarter. A metric can improve and still be red.
- Every red metric comes with an owner, a date and a decision requested from the board (budget, priority, risk acceptance) — or it does not belong in the pack.
- Definitions and targets are stable for the year. Changes are announced one quarter ahead.

## 1. MFA coverage (all users) (IDN-01)

**In plain language.** The single control that most reduces account takeover. Anything below 99 % means some accounts can be taken with a password alone. Ask what the exceptions are and when they end.

**Definition.** Share of enabled user accounts that must complete multi-factor authentication to sign in to corporate applications.

**Formula.** `enabled users with MFA enforced / enabled users x 100` — reported monthly, higher is better.

**Target example.** >= 99 %

**Watch for.** Registered is not enforced; count accounts where a policy requires MFA.

**Frameworks.** NIST CSF 2.0: PR.AA-03 · ISO 27001: A.5.17, A.8.5 · CIS v8: 6.3, 6.4

## 2. Critical vulnerabilities remediated within SLA (VUL-01)

**In plain language.** Of the most dangerous known weaknesses, how many did we fix in time. Below target means attackers have a window we have published ourselves. Ask whether the misses are concentrated on a few systems or a few teams.

**Definition.** Share of critical-severity vulnerabilities (by your internal rating, which should include exploit availability) that were fixed or compensated within the policy SLA.

**Formula.** `critical vulnerabilities closed within SLA / critical vulnerabilities due in the period x 100` — reported monthly, higher is better.

**Target example.** >= 90 % within 14 days

**Watch for.** Re-rating vulnerabilities to High to meet the Critical SLA; audit severity changes.

**Frameworks.** NIST CSF 2.0: ID.RA-01, ID.RA-08, PR.PS-02 · ISO 27001: A.8.8 · CIS v8: 7.1, 7.2, 7.4

## 3. EDR coverage (END-01)

**In plain language.** How many of our computers and servers are watched by the tool that detects and stops attacks. The gap is where an intrusion would go unseen. Ask which systems are in the gap and why.

**Definition.** Share of in-scope endpoints and servers running a healthy endpoint detection and response agent that reported in the last 7 days.

**Formula.** `devices with healthy EDR agent reporting in 7 days / devices in inventory x 100` — reported monthly, higher is better.

**Target example.** >= 98 %

**Watch for.** An installed but non-reporting agent is not coverage; use the last-seen date.

**Frameworks.** NIST CSF 2.0: DE.CM-01, DE.CM-09, PR.PS-05 · ISO 27001: A.8.7, A.8.16 · CIS v8: 10.1, 13.2

## 4. Mean time to contain (DR-02)

**In plain language.** Once we know something is wrong, how fast do we cut the attacker off. Hours matter here because damage grows with access time. Ask what the slowest case was and what delayed it.

**Definition.** Average time between an incident being declared and the attacker's access being removed or the affected asset isolated.

**Formula.** `sum of (containment time - declaration time) / incidents in the period` — reported quarterly, lower is better.

**Target example.** <= 4 hours for High and Critical incidents

**Watch for.** Containment is not resolution; a separate metric for full recovery avoids mixing the two.

**Frameworks.** NIST CSF 2.0: RS.MA-01, RS.MI-01, RS.MI-02 · ISO 27001: A.5.26 · CIS v8: 17.4, 17.7

## 5. Security incidents by severity (DR-06)

**In plain language.** What actually happened. The number of Critical incidents should be zero; a rise in lower severities often means detection improved. Ask for the one-line story of each High or Critical.

**Definition.** Number of confirmed security incidents declared in the period, broken down by severity level.

**Formula.** `count of incidents per severity in the period` — reported monthly, lower is better.

**Target example.** 0 Critical; trend of High and Medium flat or down

**Watch for.** A rising count after better detection is good news; present it with DR-04 and DR-07.

**Frameworks.** NIST CSF 2.0: RS.MA-03, GV.OV-01 · ISO 27001: A.5.24, A.5.27 · CIS v8: 17.1, 17.9

## 6. Phishing simulation click rate (AWR-01)

**In plain language.** How many of us would fall for a convincing fake email. Read it together with the report rate below; a workforce that reports is worth more than one that never clicks. Ask whether the test difficulty changed.

**Definition.** Share of recipients who clicked the link or opened the attachment in a simulated phishing campaign.

**Formula.** `recipients who clicked / emails delivered x 100` — reported monthly, lower is better.

**Target example.** <= 5 % (with difficulty level held constant)

**Watch for.** Easier templates lower the rate; record the difficulty level with every campaign.

**Frameworks.** NIST CSF 2.0: PR.AT-01 · ISO 27001: A.6.3 · CIS v8: 14.2

## 7. Tier 1 vendors assessed within cadence (TPR-01)

**In plain language.** Our most critical suppliers, checked on time. A supplier breach is our breach in the eyes of customers and regulators. Ask which critical suppliers are overdue and whether the contract gives us the right to ask.

**Definition.** Share of critical (Tier 1) vendors with a completed security assessment that is not older than the policy cadence (usually 12 months).

**Formula.** `Tier 1 vendors with a current assessment / Tier 1 vendors x 100` — reported quarterly, higher is better.

**Target example.** 100 %

**Watch for.** Re-tiering vendors down to shrink the denominator; review tier changes.

**Frameworks.** NIST CSF 2.0: GV.SC-06, GV.SC-07 · ISO 27001: A.5.19, A.5.22 · CIS v8: 15.1, 15.4, 15.5

## 8. Control coverage against framework (GOV-03)

**In plain language.** Tells the board how much of the chosen security framework is actually in place and evidenced. Movement is slow by nature; a flat line is normal, a drop means controls were removed or evidence lapsed.

**Definition.** Share of applicable framework controls (for example ISO/IEC 27001 Annex A or CIS v8 IG2) assessed as implemented and evidenced.

**Formula.** `controls implemented with evidence / applicable controls x 100` — reported quarterly, higher is better.

**Target example.** >= 85 % implemented, 100 % of Critical-priority controls

**Watch for.** Self-assessed 'implemented' without evidence is opinion, not coverage.

**Frameworks.** NIST CSF 2.0: GV.OV-01, GV.OV-03 · ISO 27001: A.5.36

## 9. Backup restore test success (CLD-04)

**In plain language.** Could we actually come back from a destructive attack. A tested restore within the agreed time is the only real proof. Ask which critical systems have never been restore-tested.

**Definition.** Share of critical systems for which a restore from backup was tested successfully, within the recovery-time objective, in the last quarter.

**Formula.** `critical systems with a successful restore test in the quarter / critical systems x 100` — reported quarterly, higher is better.

**Target example.** 100 % per year, >= 25 % per quarter on rotation

**Watch for.** A successful backup job is not a successful restore; only restores count.

**Frameworks.** NIST CSF 2.0: PR.DS-11, RC.RP-01, RC.RP-03 · ISO 27001: A.8.13, A.8.14, A.5.30 · CIS v8: 11.2, 11.3, 11.5

## 10. AI systems with a completed impact assessment (AI-02)

**In plain language.** Whether the AI we use on customers and staff was checked for harm, bias and data leakage before it went live. This is the new regulatory expectation. Ask which systems went live without one and why.

**Definition.** Share of AI systems rated medium or high impact that have a completed and approved AI impact assessment (risks to individuals, bias, data, misuse) before production use.

**Formula.** `AI systems with approved impact assessment / AI systems rated medium or high impact x 100` — reported quarterly, higher is better.

**Target example.** 100 % before go-live

**Watch for.** Assessments done after go-live still count but should be flagged; the point is before.

**Frameworks.** NIST CSF 2.0: GV.RM-01, ID.RA-01 · ISO 27001: A.5.34
